title: Stablecoins: framing the debate (speech by Pablo Hernandez de Cos, BIS General Manager, Bank of Japan seminar, Tokyo)
date_evidence: Speech header: 'Pablo Hernandez de Cos / General Manager, Bank for International Settlements / Speech at a Bank of Japan seminar / Tokyo, 20 April 2026'
key_claim: Major stablecoin issuers have already become key investors in US Treasury bills, so increased demand for government debt could lower sovereign borrowing costs at the margin and widen near-term fiscal space, but runs on stablecoins could trigger forced sales and dislocations in government bond markets; the global stablecoin market cap was around $315 billion in early April 2026, about 98% of it dollar-denominated.
frame_summary: Argues stablecoins remain a small, niche instrument whose moneyness is constrained, but whose broad adoption would carry material consequences for credit, financial stability, monetary policy and especially fiscal policy through their growing holdings of government debt.
verbatim_quote: Major stablecoin issuers have already become key investors in US Treasury bills. The increased demand for government debt could lower sovereign borrowing costs, at least at the margin, if stablecoins' demand for government bonds outweighs the reduction in demand by other market participants. As of early April 2026, the global market cap amounted to around $315 billion. And runs on stablecoins could trigger forced sales and dislocations in government bond markets. About 98% of stablecoins are denominated in dollars.
notes: Best in-window anchor for the fiscal-feedback thesis: stablecoins as a marginal sovereign-debt buyer with two-sided effects (yield relief vs fire-sale risk).

title: From money market funds to stablecoins: lessons for central banks (speech by Isabel Schnabel, ECB Executive Board, Bank of Korea International Conference, Seoul)
key_claim: Major US dollar stablecoin issuers have become sizeable holders of short-term sovereign debt, with the largest USD-pegged stablecoins now approaching the size of the largest US money market funds; USD Coin is mainly backed by sovereign bonds and repos, implying spillovers to sovereign debt markets if large redemptions force fire sales, and BIS research finds large stablecoin inflows may lower three-month US Treasury bill yields significantly with limited spillover to other tenors.
frame_summary: Argues stablecoins echo the rise of money market funds and can both run themselves and ease or tighten financial conditions via their reserve holdings, so central banks must adapt regulation, monetary-policy implementation and payment infrastructure.
verbatim_quote: major US dollar stablecoin issuers have become sizeable holders of short-term sovereign debt. BIS research finds that a large inflow into US dollar-backed stablecoins may lower three-month US Treasury bill yields significantly, with limited to no spillovers to other tenors, leading to a steepening of the yield curve. USD Coin is mainly backed by sovereign bonds and repos, which could imply spillovers to sovereign debt markets and broader fixed-income markets if large redemption requests were to force fire sales.
notes: Central-bank anchor for the run/fire-sale and yield-feedback mechanism.

title: Stablecoins and the future of money: separating functions from instruments (speech by Christine Lagarde, ECB President, Banco de Espana LatAm Economic Forum, Roda de Bara)
key_claim: Stablecoins have grown from less than USD 10 billion six years ago to more than USD 300 billion today, are overwhelmingly dollar-denominated, and nearly 90% of the market is controlled by two issuers, Tether and Circle; when retail deposits migrate into non-bank stablecoins and return to banks as wholesale funding the pass-through from policy rates to the real economy weakens, raising digital-dollarisation and monetary-sovereignty risk.
frame_summary: Argues Europe should not answer dollar stablecoins by promoting euro stablecoins but by building public settlement infrastructure anchored in central bank money, because the monetary and transmission trade-offs of stablecoins outweigh their reach gains.
verbatim_quote: Stablecoins have grown from less than USD 10 billion six years ago to more than USD 300 billion today. They are overwhelmingly denominated in US dollars, and nearly 90% of the market is controlled by two issuers - Tether and Circle. When retail deposits migrate into non-bank stablecoins and return to banks as wholesale funding, that channel narrows. Banks lend less, or less efficiently, and the pass-through from policy rates to the real economy weakens.
notes: Anchors market size, concentration and the transmission/dollarisation channel.

title: Payment Stablecoins and Cross Border Payments: Benefits and Implications for Monetary Policy Implementation (FEDS Notes, Kim, Ruprecht and Styczynski)
key_claim: The net effect of large-scale payment-stablecoin adoption on the demand for central bank reserves is hard to predict and depends on what backs the coins, and the central bank may need to recalibrate its reserve-management policy given the potentially volatile and sizable payment flows between banks and stablecoin issuers; more than 50 percent of international payments are in US dollars.
frame_summary: Argues payment stablecoins could cut intermediation costs in cross-border payments but that their effect on the Fed balance sheet and monetary-policy implementation is ambiguous and reserve-asset-dependent, possibly requiring the central bank to recalibrate reserve management.
verbatim_quote: In all of these scenarios, the central bank may need to recalibrate its reserve management policy given the potentially volatile and sizable payment flows between banks and payment stablecoin issuers. According to SWIFT data, more than 50 percent of international payments are in U.S. dollars.
notes: Anchors the monetary-policy-implementation ambiguity and reserve-management recalibration point.

title: Stablecoins and safe asset prices (BIS Working Papers No 1270, Ahmed and Aldasoro; revised June 2026, with data to March 2026)
date_evidence: Page note below the title: '(May 2025, revised in June 2026)'; abstract states 'using daily data from January 2021 to March 2026'. Cited to the June 2026 revision; original working-paper date was 28 May 2025.
key_claim: As of December 2025 dollar stablecoins' combined assets under management exceeded $270 billion, surpassing the short-term US securities holdings of major foreign investors, and in 2025 they purchased nearly $35 billion of US Treasury bills, similar to the largest US government money market funds; a $3.5 billion inflow into stablecoins lowers three-month Treasury bill yields by 0.71 basis points on impact and about 4 basis points within 10 days, with effects amplified under Treasury-market stress and as the sector scales.
frame_summary: Argues, on daily data to March 2026, that stablecoins have already become significant players in Treasury markets whose flows measurably move short-term Treasury yields, with effects that strengthen under market stress and with sector scale.
verbatim_quote: As of December 2025, their combined assets under management exceeded $270 billion, surpassing the short-term US securities holdings of major foreign investors. In 2025, they purchased nearly $35 billion of US Treasury bills, similar to the largest US government money market funds and larger than most foreign purchases. A $3.5 billion inflow lowers 3-month Treasury bill yields by 0.71 basis points on impact, and up to 4 basis points within 10 days, with limited spillovers to longer tenors.
notes: Structural anchor: canonical primary source for the quantified yield-feedback channel. Originated May 2025, revised June 2026 with data through March 2026; dated to its original publication date for transparency.

title: Making Stablecoins Stable (IMF Working Paper WP/26/74)
date_evidence: Title page: 'WP/26/74' and 'April 2026'; '(c) 2026 International Monetary Fund WP/26/74'
key_claim: Stablecoins can improve payment efficiency but are vulnerable to runs and associated welfare losses; requiring issuers to back coins with safe assets (such as central bank reserves in a narrow-bank setting) lowers run risk but trades off against issuance incentives, and a social planner can improve the equilibrium with safe-asset backing plus alternative revenue for issuers.
frame_summary: Argues, via a Diamond-Dybvig run model, that profit-maximising stablecoin issuers under-provide safety and that regulation requiring safe-asset backing is needed to lower run risk while keeping issuance viable.
verbatim_quote: they are vulnerable to runs and associated welfare losses. One way to lower run risk is to require stablecoin issuers to hold safe assets.
notes: Run-risk modelling and the narrow-bank/safe-asset-backing logic underpinning the reserve concentration in T-bills.

title: Stablecoins and the Future of Payments: Evidence from Financial Markets (IMF Working Paper WP/26/52)
date_evidence: Title page: 'WP/26/52' and 'March 2026'; '(c) 2026 International Monetary Fund WP/26/52'
key_claim: Using high-frequency market reactions to stablecoin-related legislative events, the paper finds financial-market participants expect some stablecoins to prove sufficiently credible, and that stablecoin issuance already generates positive spillovers to the US Treasury market.
frame_summary: Argues that asset-price reactions to stablecoin legislation reveal markets treat stablecoins as a credible, durable feature of the payment system rather than a passing experiment, with measurable spillovers to incumbents and to Treasury demand.
verbatim_quote: financial market participants expect (some) stablecoins to prove sufficiently credible
notes: Market-pricing corroboration that the signal is treated as durable, plus Treasury-spillover support.
